A.explanation: Gives $90 \, \Omega$ by incorrectly using $4.5 \, \text{V}$ as the p.d. across T instead of across the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor.

B.explanation: Gives $150 \, \Omega$ by assuming equal sharing of $12 \, \text{V}$, which would need $6.0 \, \text{V}$ across each resistor, not $4.5 \, \text{V}$.

C.explanation: Current $0.030 \, \text{A}$ in the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor leaves $7.5 \, \text{V}$ across T, giving $R_T = 250 \, \Omega$.

D.explanation: Gives $400 \, \Omega$ by using the ratio $12/4.5$ incorrectly to scale $150 \, \Omega$ instead of using the $7.5 \, \text{V}$ across T.

hints: Notice points X and Y are across the fixed $150 \, \Omega$ resistor, so the $4.5 \, \text{V}$ trigger voltage is the p.d. across that resistor, not across T.
Because T and the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor are in series with the $12 \, \text{V}$ supply, they carry the same current and their p.d.s add to $12 \, \text{V}$.
First find the series current from $I = V/R$ for the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor, then find the remaining p.d. across T and use $R_T = V_T/I$.
walkthrough: Identify the circuit: the $12 \, \text{V}$ supply, thermistor T and $150 \, \Omega$ resistor are in series, so the same current $I$ flows through both.
The trigger condition $V_{XY} = 4.5 \, \text{V}$ is the p.d. across the $150 \, \Omega$ resistor. So $I = V/R = 4.5/150 = 0.030 \, \text{A}$.
The p.d. across T is what is left from the supply: $V_T = 12 - 4.5 = 7.5 \, \text{V}$.
Use $R = V/I$ for T: $R_T = 7.5/0.030 = 250 \, \Omega$, with unit $\Omega$ as required.
